Automatic film dubbing aims to replace a source actor's speech with target-language dialogue that preserves se mantic meaning, temporal isochrony, vocal timbre, emo tional prosody, and visual lip synchronization. However, a systematic audit of primary dubbing literature demon strates that existing architectures optimize isolated subsets of these five objectives, inducing severe cross-modal degra dation when combined directly. Enforcing strict phoneme duration control in sequence-to-sequence translation re duces translation quality by 9.0% to 14.0% relative Sacre BLEU on CoVoST-2 (and 17.1% on pause-heavy turns), prompting large language models for viseme-compatible paraphrases degrades ASR-BLEU by 3.00 points, apply ing post-hoc voice conversion reduces intelligibility by 1.07 ASR-BLEU points, heuristic SSML emphasis lowers TTS naturalness by 0.30 MOS, and high-intensity emo tional flow-matching guidance (Sad) inflates word error rate (WER) from 11.32% to 12.12%. Conversely, large scale empirical analyses of 42,850 professional human dub lines prove that human translators do not sacrifice se mantic quality on-screen (p = 0.349), maintain moder ate speech overlap (0.658), and match exact source-target visemes in only 12.4% of on-screen speech time. Grounded in these findings, this paper presents a critical synthe sis of eight foundational dubbing studies and formulates CineDub AI, a four-stage, eight-component conceptual research framework. CineDub AI proposes: (1) a con tinuous mouth-visibility gate Mvis(t) ∈ [0,1] that inter polates allowable duration budgets Itgt( ¯ Mvis) and causal duration positional encodings between off-screen narra tion and close-ups; (2) a band-masked cross-lingual soft lip-energy attention mechanism (X-LPA) that aligns lo cal syllable jaw-opening envelopes without assuming in valid cross-lingual 1-to-1 phoneme-viseme identity; (3) a Gaussian soft-upsampled surrogate SyncNet timing loss that enables differentiable duration refinement; and (4) an articulation-gated Optimal-Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) decoder that combines deterministic consonant masks Mcons and upsampled CTC posterior en tropy ˜ HCTC with simplex-bounded source emotion priors. Finally, we specify a falsifiable, power-analyzed evaluation protocol distinguishing completed literature analysis from proposed conceptual methods and future empirical valida tion.

Developing speaking skills is one of the most challenging aspects of learning English as a foreign language (EFL). Many learners lack opportunities to communicate in English outside the classroom and face challenges such as anxiety, a lack of confidence, limited vocabulary, and difficulty formulating spontaneous speech. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new opportunities for independent speaking practice through AI-based speaking partners. This article focuses on the potential of AI partners to enhance English speaking skills, specifically highlighting platforms such as IELTS.gg (now GoPrep) and CEFRbek. The discussion centers on how AI partners can provide convenient, flexible, low-anxiety, and personalized speaking practice.

This paper studies how an AI-Based Career Recommendation System can be designed, built and deployed for students who struggle to pick a suitable academic or professional path. Because work is changing quickly with new technology, conventional counselling often cannot give guidance that is individualised, data-based and current. The proposed system uses machine learning algorithms, data mining techniques and natural language processing (NLP) models to assess a student's marks, behaviour, interests, personality and skills. Data from psychometric tests, academic records, interest inventories and career knowledge bases is combined so the system can suggest options that fit each learner's strengths and the openings in the job market. Since it detects patterns and estimates future career fit, it is expected to advise more accurately than manual counselling. The paper also stresses adaptive models that keep learning from user interactions, so suggestions improve with use. The system further seeks to lessen student uncertainty, support informed choices, and give institutions an efficient, scalable counselling service. Ultimately, the work shows that artificial intelligence can reshape career guidance, making it more individual, efficient and in step with industry trends.

The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has become central to modern healthcare by enabling continuous patient monitoring and real-time clinical decision-making, yet the rapid proliferation of connected medical devices has simultaneously expanded the attack surface and introduced serious risks to patient safety. While artificial intelligence offers strong capabilities for detecting and mitigating cyber threats, conventional centralized AI approaches often require the collection and processing of sensitive patient data, thereby recreating the very privacy risks they aim to solve. Federated learning addresses this limitation by allowing multiple devices or institutions to collaboratively train a shared model without exchanging raw data; however, it remains vulnerable to malicious or poisoned model updates from untrusted participants and still faces unresolved challenges of trust and accountability. Blockchain has been proposed as a complementary mechanism to establish decentralized trust and enhance the auditability of federated environments, although evidence of its scalability and practical feasibility in real-world healthcare settings remains limited. This paper critically examines the current landscape of security solutions at the intersection of AI, federated learning, blockchain, and IoMT. Drawing on a curated body of recent research, it maps the IoMT threat landscape across network, model, and privacy dimensions; compares AI-driven, federated, and blockchain-enabled approaches; and synthesizes findings across key technical criteria including threat coverage, detection capability, privacy protection, trust management, communication efficiency, scalability, and practical deployment feasibility. The analysis reveals three persistent gaps: inconsistent reporting practices, fragmented and heterogeneous datasets, and an unresolved tension between claimed blockchain efficiency and the limited empirical support for its scalability in real clinical environments. Notably, no existing study jointly evaluates AI, FL, and blockchain under standardized conditions that reflect a realistic hospital IoMT deployment. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a research agenda focused on real-world scalability validation, regulatory-aligned privacy standardization, 6G-integrated architectures, explainability-by-default, and quantum-resilient federated learning, with the goal of advancing IoMT security solutions that are technically robust, trustworthy, scalable, and patient-centric. Keywords : Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), federated learning, artificial intelligence, blockchain, intrusion detection, privacy-preserving machine learning.

Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered voice technologies have emerged as valuable tools in enhancing crisis communication during pandemics and disasters, yet their use in the United States (U.S.) remains fragmented. This scoping review identified and mapped evidence on AI-enabled voice intelligence for pandemic and disaster response in the U.S. and developed an evidence-informed National Voice Intelligence Emergency Preparedness Framework (NVIEPF). The review was carried out based on the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidance. The literature was searched from key bibliographic databases and grey literature sources between January 2015 and May 2026. Fifteen eligible records were synthesized using evidence mapping and thematic analysis. Current applications were primarily limited to speech recognition, automatic transcription, conversational agents, multilingual communication, and decision support in public safety communication systems. The biggest challenges were the lack of a unified communication system, the lack of consistency in implementation, limited interoperability, governance issues, cybersecurity issues, and the lack of proper evaluation in operational contexts. This research contributed to the conceptualization of the NVIEPF, which has five interconnected components that involve AI-based early warning, crisis communication, surveillance, resource coordination, and community feedback, all with human oversight. The evidence was limited by its reliance on programme reports, observational studies, and operational documentation, with limited evaluation in real-world emergency settings. Although evidence of widespread adoption of AI-driven voice technologies is limited, the framework provides a means for future research, policy development, and a phased approach to integrating AI-powered voice intelligence into the national preparedness system in the U.S.

Comparisons between machine-generated renderings and official subtitles are accumulating, yet it remains unclear where the two diverge in documentary subtitling, a genre in which the image carries part of the meaning. This review examines 25 items bearing on that question: 17 Chinese journal articles, six monographs, one dissertation, and one web source, 12 of them published after 2020, retrieved from CNKI and through reference-list tracing. Four lines of research are distinguished: comparisons of machine and human translation, the constraints of subtitling, documentary subtitle research, and translation quality assessment. Three findings emerge. First, the studies reviewed broadly agree that machine output is no longer inferior to human translation in semantic fidelity, and that its weaknesses concentrate in fluency, terminological consistency, and contextual cohesion. Second, most of these studies argue from illustrative examples rather than item-level counts and explicit criteria, so their conclusions are hard to verify. Third, research on subtitles has described the constraints of the medium in detail, and international work has turned them into computable parameters such as line limits and characters per second. A gap follows from the three. Existing comparisons treat the official translation as the sole standard, without separating genuine mistranslation from legitimate variation. The coordination of subtitles with the image, and the consistency of proper-name renderings across a whole film, has rarely been examined within the scope of this search. The review therefore proposes a three-way alignment that takes the source text and the image as joint reference, and a three-level scheme of judgement — word-and-sentence, contextual, and whole-film — counted level by level. Both are illustrated with three examples from Season 2 of the documentary The Potala Palace, in order to delimit what current large language models can and cannot achieve here.

PRIM v01 is kernel 01 of the ALADIN native-cylindrical GPU MHD Driver for Z-pinch and J×B research. It converts the conserved state (ρ, m, E) and the constrained-transport face magnetic field into primitive variables (ρ, v, p). It is one CUDA/C++ source that runs on the GPU through NVRTC and on the CPU through g++/OpenMP, in FP64 and FP32. What PRIM provides: A pressure error bound in every cell. PRIM returns b with |p − p_exact| ≤ b·p. The bound is derived by rounding-error analysis, with its assumptions stated, and verified numerically against an 80-bit oracle in both the normal and the subnormal range. A cell is flagged UNRESOLVED when p keeps fewer than 3 significant digits, as happens at low plasma β. Refusal instead of floors. Three kinds of cell are refused, with NaN outputs and a flag: non-positive density or any non-finite input; total energy below kinetic plus magnetic energy; finite inputs whose intermediates overflow. The adiabatic index must satisfy 1 < γ ≤ 2. An explicit flag policy for the Driver, consistent with HLLD v05.1. A consistent cell-centred field. It is the constrained-transport face average, the same one HLLD v05.1 and UCT-EMF v02 use. Bit-identical GPU and CPU results, including the subnormal range. An inverse, conserved(), which converts primitive variables back to the conserved state. Results (campaign PRIM-01, run 4): GPU leg (NVIDIA L4) 17 / 17 VERIFIED; CPU leg 11 / 11 VERIFIED. compute-sanitizer: 0 errors and 0 hazards. The pressure bound is never exceeded. The worst case uses 0.32 of the bound over 758 733 normal-range cells (ρ from 1e-8 to 1e8, β from 1e-12 to 1e6) and 0.29 over 375 k underflow-range cells. Every velocity is the correctly rounded m/ρ. Refusal is exact and local, and overflow is refused. GPU = CPU bit for bit, in the normal and the subnormal range. The README normalised Z-pinch is recovered to 1.1e-16, and HLLD fed with PRIM’s output keeps exact balance. In FP32, p keeps 3 digits only down to β ≈ 1e-4; in FP64, down to β ≈ 1e-12. Development record: publication review of run 1 led to overflow refusal, γ validation, underflow terms in the bound and the written derivation (run 2). Run 2 then failed in FP32 on the GPU. Diagnosis traced the failure to CuPy’s RawModule, which appends -ftz=true after user options and so flushes FP32 subnormals whatever the user passes. Run 4 compiles through NVRTC directly and checks the PTX. All runs and probes are preserved. The bundle contains the kernel, the independent oracle, the campaign with predeclared thresholds, both legs’ results, the sanitizer logs, the Driver adapter, the README benchmark, the full history, and the verification report. Calibration of advanced soil constitutive models remains challenging because multiple parameters jointly control stress–strain responses. In practice, these parameters are often determined by manual trial and error from a few laboratory tests, leaving two questions unanswered: whether the fitted parameters are identifiable and which additional test would best reduce the remaining ambiguity. A parameter set may therefore reproduce the available data yet remain non-unique, leading to divergent predictions under untested conditions. In this work, we develop a human-supervised agentic-AI calibrate–diagnose–suggest workflow for parameter identification in soil constitutive models. The workflow combines gradient-based parameter estimation, Fisher-information-based diagnosis of weak parameter directions, and a large language model (LLM) agent that translates the weakest Fisher direction into a targeted follow-up laboratory test. This translation is guided by an LLM-organized parameter–response map, which is checked against established expert guidance. We demonstrate the workflow using NorSand in eight simulator-generated triaxial scenarios spanning drainage conditions, density states, and confining pressures. A single agent-suggested follow-up test substantially reduces the broad multi-parameter ambiguity left by single-test calibration: excluding one weakly observable parameter, the median relative error is 0.17%, and Fisher information analysis indicates improved local identifiability in all eight scenarios. The workflow also exposes the parameter that fit-only calibration would leave weakly constrained. We further find that a complementary test selected retrospectively from published data reduces local ambiguity in the targeted parameter combination. These findings show that agentic AI can support auditable calibration by turning numerical identifiability diagnosis into actionable decisions.

Background Effective communication is a core competency in medical education, but traditional training is resource-intensive and hard to scale. Virtual patients based on large language models (LLMs) may help, yet evidence on their usability and perceived value outside English-language settings is limited. Methods In this cross-sectional pilot study, 102 medical students at the University of Málaga completed two Spanish-language history-taking encounters with a GPT-4-based virtual patient and received automated feedback. They completed an anonymous, self-developed questionnaire (0–10 ratings and open-ended questions). Analyses were descriptive, plus an exploratory logistic regression of gender on perceived training need. Results Participants were mostly women (73.5%) and fourth-year students (85.3%). 86.3% (88/102) rated the tool easy or very easy to use and 60.8% (62/102) reported no need for prior training. Most feedback statements had mean ratings of 7.4 or more (0–10), highest for usefulness in exploring the reason for consultation and the patient's history (8.3); agreement that AI feedback does not replace tutors was moderate (6.14). Women were less likely than men to report needing prior training (OR: 0.29, 95% CI: 0.11–0.73; exploratory hypothesis-generating). Free-text comments ( n = 33) valued realism, interaction and feedback depth, and noted limited case variety and no nonverbal communication. Conclusions Students found the LLM-based virtual patient easy to use and its feedback useful. Given the lack of a comparison group, non-validated self-report measures, a single site and co-first authors affiliation with the developer, the findings indicate acceptability and perceived value only, not effectiveness. Controlled studies with validated, observer-rated outcomes are needed.

Existing research has demonstrated the benefits and envisioned broader applications of using extended reality (XR) head-mounted displays (HMDs) to create virtual display extensions for personal computers (PCs), offering a more flexible and cost-effective alternative to traditional physical monitors. This combined setup, with inputs from both sources available, provides users with more options for interaction. In this work, we aim to understand the advantages and disadvantages of these inputs and their interaction techniques in the fundamental window placement tasks in virtual displays enabled by the combined use of a PC and an HMD. With their standard inputs, we identified five potential hand-based window placement techniques: Mouse Cursor, Pinch Drag, Keyboard Shortcut, Touchpad Gesture, and Wrist Bending. We conducted a mixed-design user study (N = 40) to evaluate user performance and experience with these window placement techniques in two display setups: a fully virtual setup where the HMD displays all windows, and a hybrid setup involving a laptop screen in addition to the HMD’s virtual windows. All five techniques were evaluated in a structured layout task, while Mouse Cursor and Pinch Drag were additionally compared in a freeform placement task. Across both setups, Mouse Cursor was faster than Pinch Drag, while Keyboard Shortcut and Touchpad Gesture were faster and produced fewer failed trials than Wrist Bending. Laptop-based techniques also received higher usability ratings and lower perceived workload ratings than mid-air techniques. Nevertheless, some participants preferred mid-air techniques, valuing their naturalness. Our empirical findings can guide the future design of cross-device and cross-reality interactions between XR HMDs and PCs.

Purpose: This study examined the effects of learning motivation, behavioral engagement, cognitive engagement, emotional engagement, agentic engagement, and feedback on college students’ learning performance in physical education. Research design, data and methodology: This study adopted a mixed-methods action research design. The questionnaire was developed based on established literature, and content validity was assessed using the Index of Item-Objective Congruence. Reliability was confirmed through a pilot test with 30 students using Cronbach’s alpha. Quantitative data were collected from 169 valid questionnaires administered to undergraduate students at Guizhou University and analyzed using multiple linear regression to examine relationships between the variables. Based on the regression results and qualitative insights from student interviews, an eight-week Intervention Design Implementation was conducted with 30 students. Paired-sample t-tests were used to compare pre-intervention and post-intervention results. Results: The multiple linear regression analysis indicated that emotional engagement (β = 0.437) and feedback (β = 0.572) had significant positive effects on learning performance, while the other variables showed no significant direct effects. The paired-sample t-test results revealed significant improvements across all variables, including learning performance, after the intervention. Conclusions: The findings suggest that integrating emotional engagement, feedback, and supportive intervention activities can effectively enhance learning performance and support the development of sustained physical exercise habits among college students.

Prospective students and their parents need quick and reliable answers about admissions, fees, courses, eligibility, scholarships, hostels and placements, yet most college help desks work only during oﬃce hours and depend on staff who answer the same questions again and again. This paper presents the design and development of an AI-Based College Enquiry Chatbot System that answers such enquiries automatically through a conversational web interface that is available round the clock. The system combines natural language processing with machine learning. Each user message is pre-processed (tokenisation, normalisation, stop-word removal and lemmatisation), converted into TF-IDF and sentence-embedding features, and mapped to one of twelve enquiry intents by a Support Vector Machine classifier. A dialogue manager then retrieves the verified answer from a structured knowledge base, so that fees, dates and eligibility rules are never invented by the model. Queries classified with low confidence are passed to a fallback module that suggests related questions or forwards the enquiry to college staff, and an administrator dashboard allows the knowledge base to be updated without changing any code. Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Random Forest and SVM classifiers were compared, and the embedding-based SVM gave the best cross-validated accuracy of 94.2% with an average response time below half a second. The proposed system reduces the workload of the admission oﬃce, shortens the waiting time of applicants and offers a scalable, low-cost decision- support tool for educational institutions.

Digital transformation requires employees to develop digital technical competence and understand the use and limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in their work. This study examines the roles of digital technical competence and AI literacy in supporting asset management at PT Lancar Wiguna Sejahtera (Lawson), a retail company. A qualitative case study approach was employed, with data collected through interviews involving five informants representing asset administration, store operations, information technology, area supervision, and maintenance functions. The findings indicate that digital technical competence supports the use of internal applications, asset recording, reporting, information verification, and asset status updates. However, the asset management process still faces challenges related to incomplete information, delayed reporting, discrepancies between administrative records and actual asset conditions, and limited visibility of follow-up status. AI literacy involves understanding AI capabilities and limitations, evaluating AI-generated outputs, and protecting confidential company information. The interviews indicate that AI is considered a potential tool for summarizing reports and organizing information, but its outputs require verification against official company records, field conditions, technical knowledge, and operational procedures. No evidence was found that AI had been integrated into the company's official asset management system or used for predictive maintenance. The study highlights the importance of task-based training, mentoring, standardized reporting procedures, information security awareness, and coordination among organizational roles to support more effective asset management.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the field of analytics, understood as the continuum from descriptive business intelligence to predictive and prescriptive analytics augmented by machine learning. While organizations are acquiring these systems on a massive scale, the persistent gap between equipment rates and actual usage rates remains largely unexplained. The frameworks inherited from information systems adoption research (the technology acceptance model, the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology, the technology-organization-environment framework, and the diffusion of innovations) were built for systems governed by explicit and auditable rules; their relevance to opaque, partially agentic, and ethically problematic systems has not been systematically examined. This article maps the factors of analytics adoption in the age of AI. The corpus derives from a scoping review that was reported following the PRISMA-ScR protocol: 16,113 records identified, 11,170 screened, 1097 assessed for eligibility, and 42 articles analyzed. The corpus was processed through inductive qualitative content analysis following the Gioia methodology. Coding yielded 106 first-order concepts, 18 s-order themes, and 6 aggregate dimensions. The reliability of the categorization was checked through independent double coding of 18.9% of the coding units: raw agreement reached 80.0%, and Cohen’s kappa was 0.79. The most frequently discussed factors are not the performance attributes of the technology but the socio-organizational and epistemic conditions of its appropriation. The article proposes a moderated mediation model built on three layers: the enabling layer occupies the position of antecedent; the legitimating layer, specific to the age of AI, that of mediator and bottleneck of adoption; and the two dimensions of the actualizing layer that of moderators.

documents.abstract: Why do female leaders face professional penalties for the same expressions of anger that often benefit male leaders? Despite decades of research, gender bias in leadership evaluations remains a stubborn hurdle for women seeking career advancement. In this theoretical paper, I develop a stereotype-context competition model to explain how gender bias arises in the evaluation of leaders who express anger, and to identify conditions under which such bias is less likely to occur. I argue that evaluations of angry leaders are shaped by two competing forces: a pro-bias force driven by stereotype information and a counter-bias force driven by contextual information. I further propose that the pro-bias force generally prevails, resulting in the persistence of gender bias in initial evaluations of angry leaders. Finally, I identify three categories of factors—related to the leader, the observer, and the situation—that can reduce the likelihood of gender bias. I conclude by discussing the theoretical and practical implications of the model.

The Euratom-funded project DORADO (Digital Twins and Ontology for Robot-Assisted Decommissioning Operations) aims to improve safety, efficiency, and sustainability in nuclear decommissioning through the integration of advanced digital technologies. Building on the foundations established in the earlier PLEIADES project, DORADO is developing a holistic digital platform that combines Building Information Modelling (BIM), digital twins (DTs), robotics, sensor-data fusion, ontology-based knowledge management, and artificial intelligence (AI) within a unified data-driven framework for decommissioning operations. The DORADO architecture is centred on a secure common data environment that uses the Digital Twin Exchange Standard (DTXS) to enable real-time communication between distributed modules and digital assets. Emphasis is placed on AI-enabled methods for autonomous decision support, hazard identification, mission planning, and adaptive radiological assessment. AI and machine-learning methods are being developed to support automated point-cloud change detection, predictive updating of digital twins, optimisation of robotic inspection routes, integration of measurement data, and intelligent voice-assisted reporting for field operators. The integrated technologies will be demonstrated using operational datasets from nuclear facilities in Finland, Norway, Belgium, and Lithuania, including applications in radiological characterisation, ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) dose estimation, robotic inspection, waste monitoring, and dynamic BIM updating. Once completed, the DORADO platform is expected to reduce worker radiation exposure, improve situational awareness, strengthen long-term knowledge management, and support safer and more cost-effective nuclear decommissioning practices.

When a viewer reports that they trust a visualization, what have we measured? Trust measurement in visualization has improved: validated multidimensional inventories are replacing single-item ratings. This position paper argues that level measures answer only part of the question that matters for design. They record how much a person trusts, not whether that trust is warranted or how it changes with use. Research on trust in automation and AI-assisted decision making has long treated calibration, the fit between trust and trustworthiness, as the target. We ask whether that agenda shapes how visualization studies measure trust. Auditing sixteen recent journal studies, six from visualization and ten from an adjacent services literature, we find three gaps. The construct is fragmented. Where visualization experiments record what trust could be judged against, they use different referents and rarely analyse trust against them; the services studies record none. And no design follows trust through failure and repair. We argue that calibration should supplement level measures, identify what trust in a visualization can be calibrated against, and specify the metrics and designs this requires.

This record contains a complete, ready-to-deliver half-day training package on the practical and responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in medical research, developed for clinicians and researchers at Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Mekelle University. The 32-slide presentation, scheduled from 08:30 to 12:30 with a coffee break, guides participants through the research lifecycle in seven sessions covering AI foundations and prompting, literature searching and study design, academic writing and publishing, qualitative and quantitative data analysis, and ethics, privacy, and verification. Each stage includes realistic, ready-to-use prompt examples for tools such as ChatGPT, PubMed, Google Scholar, and Elicit, alongside live demonstrations of AI-assisted statistical analysis using Stata and R. No technical background is assumed. All acronyms, including AI, ML, LLM, NLP, RAG, PICO/PICOT, PRISMA, and ICMJE, are spelled out and explained in plain language. Relevant research reporting standards, including STROBE, CONSORT, PRISMA, CARE, and EQUATOR, are also introduced at the appropriate stages. To encourage active participation, the training incorporates three hands-on activities: identifying fabricated references, improving an academic abstract, and completing a 20-minute research sprint. The presentation concludes with a two-slide glossary and a verified reference list. Every slide includes detailed, structured speaker notes covering the opening, explanation, practical example, key message, transition, and presenter guidance. This enables any facilitator, including those without a medical or informatics background, to deliver the training confidently. A companion trainer's workbook is also included in this record, containing the training run sheet, timed talking points, demonstration runbooks, activity answer keys, a question-and-answer bank, and a pronunciation guide. All scenarios, quotations, and datasets used throughout the training are fictional or synthetic, ensuring that no real patient information is used. The training consistently emphasises the importance of human oversight and responsible AI use: AI provides drafts and assistance; researchers remain responsible for decisions, verification, and final outputs.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming crime prevention by improving intelligence gathering, predictive policing, digital forensics, financial crime detection, and border security. In Nigeria, however, the adoption of AI within the security sector remains limited despite growing security challenges such as cybercrime, terrorism, financial crime, kidnapping, and transnational organized crime. This paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and future directions of AI for crime prevention in Nigeria through a review of conceptual, theoretical, and empirical literature. Routine Activity Theory provides the theoretical framework by explaining how AI strengthens capable guardianship through enhanced surveillance, predictive analytics, and intelligence-led policing. The review indicates that AI can significantly improve crime detection, operational efficiency, and evidence-based decision-making when supported by robust digital infrastructure, effective governance, skilled personnel, and appropriate legal and ethical frameworks. Nevertheless, challenges including inadequate technological infrastructure, limited institutional capacity, regulatory gaps, algorithmic bias, and data privacy concerns continue to hinder its effective deployment. The paper concludes that AI can complement traditional policing style when deployed responsibly, and can significantly enhance Nigeria's national security architecture. It recommends strengthening Nigeria's national artificial intelligence strategy, investing in digital infrastructure, enhancing AI literacy within security agencies, promoting inter-agency collaboration, and establishing comprehensive governance frameworks to ensure the responsible integration of AI into national crime prevention. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Border Security, Crime Prevention, Financial Crime, National Security.

documents.abstract: Heart failure affects more than 64 million people worldwide and remains associated with high mortality and recurrent hospitalisation. Artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models (LLMs), is being evaluated across the care pathway, but evidence maturity varies by task. The aim of this narrative review was to appraise direct evidence for LLM applications in heart failure, distinguish it from supporting evidence for other AI methods and propose a risk-based framework for clinical evaluation and governance. The strongest direct LLM evidence concerns electronic health record extraction, document drafting, patient information and clinical trial endpoint adjudication. A small, randomised pilot evaluated supervised generative-AI-guided optimisation of guideline-directed medical therapy. Prospective case-finding and monitoring evidence largely concerns non-LLM AI. For conversational AI telemonitoring (a natural language interface with rule-based alerting), prospective evidence was limited to a single non-randomised controlled pilot. Performance depends on task definition, data completeness, human review and workflow adoption. Overall, LLMs can support clearly defined, supervised heart failure tasks, but current evidence does not justify autonomous high-stakes care. The evidence base is expanding but predominantly retrospective. Prospective trials, disease-specific benchmarks, equity assessment and regulatory engagement are prerequisites for safe clinical translation. Human oversight remains essential across all current-generation applications.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing pharmacy practice by facilitating the analysis of large amounts of clinical and pharmaceutical data, aiding medication management, strengthening medication safety and encouraging patient-centred care. The traditional role of the pharmacist in dispensing and supply is being transformed into that of clinical decision making, medication optimization, therapeutic monitoring and individualized care. This review discusses the major applications of AI in pharmacy and the changing role of pharmacists in AI-assisted clinical practice. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, generative AI and AI-enabled clinical decision-support systems have shown promise in prescription screening, detection of drug–drug interactions and prediction of adverse drug events, decrease in medication errors, dose optimization and personalized pharmacotherapy. These tools can also help streamline workflow and save time for pharmacists to focus on clinical interventions and patient counseling by taking on repetitive data-heavy tasks. However, pharmacists remain indispensable for clinical interpretation, ethical reasoning, patient-specific assessment, and final therapeutic decisions, so the successful implementation relies on effective human–AI collaboration. The uptake of AI also brings concerns around data privacy, algorithmic bias, professional responsibility, legal uncertainty, transparency and patient safety and pharmacy education will need to incorporate digital skills and AI literacy into pharmacist training. AI with appropriate oversight by humans, ethical safeguards and robust regulation can enhance pharmacy practice and facilitate the transition of pharmacists from medication dispensers to AI-assisted clinical decision-makers.

documents.abstract: Chronic liver disease, particularly cirrhosis, produces a fragile, rebalanced hemostatic state. Patients may develop bleeding or thrombosis. The international normalized ratio and platelet count incompletely reflect concurrent procoagulant and anticoagulant changes and poorly predict procedural bleeding. Viscoelastic testing and thrombin-generation assays assess hemostasis more broadly. Randomized trials support viscoelastic testing-guided reductions in blood product use, but these trials do not establish prediction of later bleeding or thrombosis. Machine-learning models address gastrointestinal bleeding outcomes, variceal hemorrhage, portal vein thrombosis (PVT), and transfusion requirements using clinical records, imaging, or elastography. Most cirrhosis models address one outcome, omit direct hemostatic measurements, and have limited external validation. Within the English-language eligibility criteria and focused queries of a PubMed update on July 29, 2026, no adult model jointly estimating future bleeding and PVT in cirrhosis was identified. This structured narrative minireview evaluates the evidence for both outcomes and specifies research requirements for paired-risk models and a possible digital twin of the coagulation-portal axis. Treatment-specific predictions would require additional causal validation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly emerged as a promising resource for supporting students with dyslexia. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature examines AI primarily as an assistive technology, with limited attention to the cognitive mechanisms through which it may enhance reading development. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework that integrates Baddeley’s multicomponent model of working memory with contemporary AI-supported educational tools. Drawing on research in cognitive psychology, special education, cognitive load theory, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and self-determination theory, the paper argues that AI should be understood not merely as an instructional aid but as an external cognitive support system that complements and extends the functional capacity of working memory during reading. Specifically, the framework illustrates how AI technologies—including text-to-speech systems, speech recognition, adaptive learning environments, and generative AI applications—may reduce cognitive load while supporting the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, and episodic buffer. Through this cognitive alignment, AI has the potential to facilitate decoding, comprehension, learner engagement, and reading autonomy among students with dyslexia. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded perspective that connects cognitive theory with emerging educational technologies. Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of a specific intervention, the paper provides an integrative model to guide future empirical research, instructional design, and the development of AI-supported reading interventions for learners with dyslexia.

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with a long preclinical phase, making early biomarker discovery essential for timely diagnosis, risk stratification, and intervention. Hearing loss has increasingly been recognized as a clinically important and potentially modifiable factor associated with cognitive decline and dementia risk. Beyond peripheral auditory impairment, accumulating evidence suggests that central auditory dysfunction, altered auditory processing, and electrophysiological abnormalities may emerge during the course of AD and related cognitive disorders. Auditory electrophysiological signals, including electroencephalography (EEG), auditory event-related potentials (ERP), auditory evoked cortical potentials (AECP), auditory brainstem response (ABR) recordings, cochlear microphonics (CM), and distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) measures, provide objective and repeatable measurements of peripheral and central auditory pathway function. However, conventional analysis based on peak latency, amplitude, spectral power, and manually engineered features may not fully capture subtle disease-related alterations distributed across time, frequency, and waveform morphology. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to extract high-dimensional and physiologically informative representations from auditory and neural signals. Machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), self-supervised learning (SSL), explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and multimodal modeling can support data-driven biomarker discovery, especially in settings where labeled datasets are limited and electrophysiological changes are subtle. This critical narrative review synthesizes current knowledge at the intersection of hearing loss, AD, auditory electrophysiology, and AI. We discuss traditional signal processing, supervised ML, deep neural networks, self-supervised representation learning, explainable models, and multimodal integration strategies. We also identify major methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, heterogeneous acquisition protocols, insufficient external validation, limited interpretability, data leakage risks, and challenges in translating animal-model findings to human disease. Finally, we propose future directions for trustworthy, interpretable, and multimodal AI systems capable of advancing auditory electrophysiological biomarkers for AD and hearing-related neurodegeneration.

Artificial intelligence supports Chinese ancient-book preservation through image restoration, document understanding, and knowledge services. This review synthesizes advances using a three-tier architecture and proposes a six-dimensional conceptual framework informed by findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability. Generative restoration, multimodal recognition, and knowledge-grounded generation show promise, while unsupported reconstructions, data scarcity, and limited evaluation constrain reliability. Priorities include evidence traceability, human oversight, and domain-specific evaluation.

Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes that avoid hazard rather than merely control it after the fact, reconsidering reactions, solvents, catalysts and materials from the earliest stages of design.Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly part of this effort because it offers a practical way to make sense of the very large volumes of chemical and environmental data modern research now generates.Machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, natural language processing and computer vision are being used to anticipate reaction outcomes, screen catalysts and solvents, flag likely toxicity or persistence, and interpret environmental sensor data in near real time.This chapter surveys these applications, from predictive chemistry and multi-objective process optimisation to safer molecular design, catalyst and solvent screening, biocatalysis, sustainable materials, carbon capture, green analytical chemistry, and the monitoring of water, air and waste.It maps AI onto the twelve principles of green chemistry, and argues that AI's own computational footprint means it cannot be assumed sustainable simply because it accelerates discovery.A responsible approach requires trustworthy data, inspectable models, rigorous experimental validation, life-cycle thinking, and honest accounting of the energy AI itself consumes.The chapter closes with a practical ten-step framework, arguing that AI's durable contribution to sustainability will come from its disciplined integration with chemical judgement, safety practice and environmental accountability -not from computational power alone.

Background Postoperative outcomes in pediatric urology vary substantially despite generally high procedural success, creating a need for more individualized risk prediction. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to integrate clinical, anatomical, laboratory, imaging, and perioperative data, but the breadth, methodological strength, and clinical readiness of current prediction models remain unclear. Objective To map AI and machine-learning models predicting postoperative complications and outcomes in pediatric urology by characterizing procedures, prediction targets, predictor domains, model types, validation strategies, explainability, and clinical readiness, and to identify priorities for future validation and clinical implementation. Methods Six databases were searched through 20 July 2026. Eligible studies developed, validated, compared, or evaluated an individual-level AI/ML model predicting an outcome after a pediatric urologic procedure or kidney transplantation. Evidence was synthesized narratively by clinical domain, prediction target, predictor domain, model family, and validation level; no meta-analysis was performed. Results Of 1,478 records identified through the database searches, 25 studies (40 prediction tasks, six clinical domains) met eligibility. All were retrospective. Kidney transplantation contributed the most studies (n=8); stone disease contributed the most tasks (n=13). Machine-learning models based on tree ensembles and boosting (e.g., random forest, gradient boosting) were selected in 24/40 tasks (60.0%). Among 24 tasks reporting AUC, values ranged 0.559–0.970 (14/24, 58.3% ≥0.80), but several favorable estimates rested on very few outcome events. Only two studies (8%) performed independent external validation; calibration was reported in four studies (16%) and decision-curve analysis in seven (28%). No study prospectively evaluated a model, embedded it into routine care, or assessed patient benefit or fairness. Conclusion AI-based postoperative prediction in pediatric urology is expanding and targets clinically important outcomes, with several models showing promising discrimination for individualized risk stratification. However, current evidence remains at an early stage, with predominantly retrospective, single-center studies. Multicenter external validation, standardized outcome definitions, calibration reporting, dynamic multimodal modeling, and prospective impact evaluation are needed before these tools can be considered ready for routine pediatric urologic practice.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in career guidance, occupational recommendation, and candidate-job matching, yet these applications are often treated as interchangeable despite serving different stakeholders and creating distinct downstream risks. This structured methodological review examines how AI methods are evaluated across career matching and algorithmic trustworthiness. Two semantic searches identified 980 unique records, of which 181 studies published in 2020–2026 met the extraction criteria under screening. We purposively selected 19 primary studies for in-depth analysis. Although the field has grown rapidly (62.4% of candidate studies appeared in 2025–2026), the close-read studies show that model performance depends heavily on proxy labels and validation design. High offline performance (area under the curve (AUC) > 0.92) did not consistently translate into robust outcomes: performance degraded for job seekers with few recorded work experiences, a graph baseline reached an AUC of only 0.641, and multimodal interview scoring added negligible predictive gain over text (Spearman ρ = 0.46 vs 0.45) while visual features showed adverse impact (ratio: 0.52). The advantage of fair re-ranking narrowed as employers made more selections, and screeners conformed more often to incorrect recommendations from a bag-of-words model than from a neural model. These findings demonstrate the limitations of static offline metrics. We propose a four-level evaluation framework addressing representation validity, decision-stage stress-testing, human-AI interaction, and consequential impact. Because retrieval was incomplete and inclusion decisions were not independently re-adjudicated, this review assesses methodological practices rather than claiming an exhaustive census.

documents.abstract: Modern children are growing up in a digital world that offers immense potential, with many beginning to use technology from an early age. This digital environment presents countless opportunities for learning and development, but it also necessitates a balanced, thoughtful approach to raising children as informed, open-minded citizens. Industry 4.0, driven by artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT), is reshaping how children think, learn, and interact with the world. The integration of AI into children's lives is a complex issue, bringing both significant benefits and notable risks. On the positive side, AI can power educational tools, interactive games, and personalized learning experiences, fostering cognitive development and creativity. However, it also introduces serious concerns, such as exposure to cyber threats, potential manipulation, privacy violations through data collection, and increased access to harmful content. This study explores the dual impact of information technologies on children's digital development. It examines the primary cybersecurity challenges children face and assesses how AI can both enhance and jeopardize their well-being. By analyzing these multifaceted dynamics, the research aims to offer recommendations for maximizing the advantages of the digital age while ensuring a safer and more supportive online environment for children.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is incorporated into frameworks for teaching, learning, assessment, and educational organization. This critical integrative review examines how these frameworks accommodate AI and the evidence associated with their use. The review used purposive web searches and included publications available by mid-October 2026. The synthesis distinguishes application, contextual specification, construct extension, relational reconfiguration, and AI-specific synthesis across professional knowledge, curriculum, learning, design, inclusion, assessment, and adoption. A source-to-entry crosswalk documents 120 analytical entries linked to 123 publications. Thirty empirical reports and one design case receive a structured access and appraisal record. All 31 selected records were examined in full text. Framework classifications based on partial material remain provisional. The comparison identifies tensions concerning ethical judgment, allocation of cognitive work, and attribution of understanding. Reported competence, AI-assisted products, and independent performance support different educational claims. A worked construct crosswalk shows how agency, regulation, and ethical judgment require distinct units and observations. Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) provides disciplinary examples within a broader educational scope. The resulting research priorities connect proposed conceptual changes with the evidence needed to examine them.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an influential factor in contemporary English language teaching because it expands access to feedback, practice, and personalised learning support. This article examines the role of artificial intelligence in English language teaching and analyses innovative learning approaches associated with its integration. The study is based on a qualitative review of recent academic and policy literature. The findings indicate that AI contributes most visibly to speaking practice, writing support, adaptive learning, learner autonomy, and classroom innovation. At the same time, the literature highlights important challenges, including ethical concerns, overreliance on technology, limited teacher preparation, and the need to preserve meaningful human interaction in the learning process. The article concludes that artificial intelligence should be used not as a replacement for the teacher, but as a pedagogical resource that becomes effective only when integrated critically, ethically, and methodologically.

Research monograph (working paper, not peer reviewed), 58 pages, 52 references. Background. Around one in six people experience infertility, more than three million IVF cycles are reported annually and an estimated 13 to 17 million children have been born through IVF. Artificial intelligence (AI) is now applied along the entire IVF pathway while its clinical benefit remains contested. Aim. To provide an integrated, critical assessment of AI in IVF as of late 2026 across clinical evidence, market development, regulation and ethics, and to derive scenario-based predictions and recommendations. Methods. Structured narrative review, documentary analysis of EU, Swiss, UK and US regulation, secondary analysis of market data, normative ethical analysis and scenario analysis. Results. AI embryo assessment is roughly ten times faster than manual assessment, but the largest randomised trial (n = 1,066) did not demonstrate noninferiority on clinical pregnancy (46.5% vs 48.2%), and time-lapse imaging did not improve live birth in a trial of more than 1,500 patients. The AI embryo selection market is estimated at USD 320 million in 2025, growing about 18.5% annually. Under the EU AI Act most clinical IVF AI is high-risk. Polygenic embryo screening is considered not ready for clinical practice by the ASRM. Conclusions. The study proposes the cohort constraint as an explanatory principle, a four-question governance framework for clinics, ten falsifiable predictions to 2031 and a research agenda. AI should inform and accelerate; accountable humans should decide. Use of AI: an AI language model assisted with literature synthesis, structuring and language editing; the author verified all sources and takes full responsibility.

documents.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research is changing how data are analysed, hypotheses are generated, and explanations are developed. Algorithmic systems increasingly participate in operations previously carried out directly by researchers. Their contribution, however, raises a methodological question: under what conditions can AI-generated outputs be regarded as justified scientific results rather than merely useful information? This paper examines the capabilities and limitations of AI in scientific inquiry, focusing on the distinction between statistical regularities and causal explanation, the validation of hypotheses, scientific understanding, reproducibility, and researchers' epistemic autonomy. The conceptual basis of this analysis is the distinction between participation in cognitive operations and independent epistemic subjecthood. In the extended-mind approach, external resources may become functionally integrated into human cognition. AI-assisted research likewise involves a distribution of cognitive operations between researchers and algorithmic systems.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is growing faster than ever and changing many parts of our lives. At the same time, emotional intelligence (EI) remains a key human skill that guides our decisions, relationships, and ethical choices. However, there is a growing tension between the strengths of AI and the unique abilities of EI. This article examines how AI and EI interact and sometimes clash, focusing on the balance between technological efficiency and human empathy. By analyzing examples from business, education, and everyday life, the article shows that neither AI nor EI alone can solve all problems. Instead, the future depends on combining the speed and logic of AI with the understanding and insight of EI. Understanding this balance is essential for creating a society that is both advanced and truly human-centered.

documents.abstract: The disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 on March 8, 2014, remains one of the most complex and unresolved aviation mysteries of the twenty-first century. Despite extensive international search operations, satellite communication analysis, radar investigations, and oceanographic modeling, the aircraft’s final location and the precise causes of its disappearance remain uncertain. This research proposal explores the potential application of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to re-examine existing MH370-related data and generate new analytical perspectives. The proposed study aims to integrate machine learning, deep learning, geographic information systems (GIS), and probabilistic modeling to analyze multiple sources of evidence, including satellite handshake data, flight trajectory information, aircraft performance parameters, meteorological conditions, ocean current patterns, and recovered debris locations. AI algorithms may identify hidden patterns, detect anomalies, and evaluate alternative flight-path scenarios that may have been overlooked through conventional analytical approaches. It examines AI as an advanced decision-support tool that can enhance forensic aviation investigation. The study addresses challenges associated with incomplete datasets, algorithmic uncertainty, transparency, and ethical communication with victims’ families and the public. By developing an interdisciplinary AI-based investigation framework, this research contributes to aviation safety science, forensic data analysis, and future disaster investigation methodologies.

This study examines how artificial intelligence-driven assessment systems shape examination integrity across Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) Computer-Based Test (CBT) centres in Nigeria. The study adopted a cross-sectional survey design and drew on a sample of 400 respondents comprising CBT centre supervisors, invigilators, technical officers and returning candidates, selected through multistage sampling across six geopolitical zones. Data were gathered with a structured questionnaire whose reliability returned a Cronbach's alpha of 0.87, and were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The findings indicate that AI biometric authentication, AI-enabled remote proctoring and AI anomaly detection each exert a positive and statistically significant effect on examination integrity, with the combined model explaining roughly 61 per cent of the variance in integrity outcomes. Infrastructure reliability and invigilator digital literacy emerged as meaningful conditioning factors. The study concludes that AI systems have measurably strengthened the credibility of JAMB examinations, though their gains remain hostage to power supply, connectivity and human capacity. Recommendations centre on infrastructure investment, sustained capacity-building and a transparent governance framework for algorithmic decision-making in high-stakes assessment

Wound care requires accurate assessment, infection prevention, appropriate treatment selection and longitudinal monitoring. Medicinal plants contain diverse phytochemicals with potential antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and tissue-repair activities. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to plant recognition, natural-product discovery and digital wound assessment. Yet the translation of AI-generated botanical predictions into safe nursing practice remains poorly integrated. An integrative evidence review was developed from identifiable peer-reviewed reviews and primary-source records located through online scholarly sources. Evidence was grouped into medicinal-plant image recognition, AI-enabled natural-product discovery, clinical herbal wound interventions, and AI-supported nursing/wound assessment. The synthesis distinguishes computational, laboratory/preclinical and human clinical evidence. A systematic review of deep learning for medicinal-plant recognition included 31 studies; 67.7% used private datasets, 96.7% used leaf organs, 83.8% used transfer learning and 64.5% used convolutional neural networks. A separate clinical review identified 26 herbal wound trials involving 45 plant species. A natural-product review describes AI applications in activity prediction and candidate discovery while emphasising dataset quality and validation. AI may support species screening, phytochemical prioritisation and wound monitoring, but predictions must be validated through botanical authentication, chemical characterisation, experimental testing and controlled clinical studies. Nurses should use only appropriately quality-assured products and validated decision-support tools, retaining professional judgement and patient-centred accountability.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into modern justice systems, influencing decision-making in criminal justice, hiring, surveillance, healthcare, and public administration. Although AI promises efficiency and consistency, a growing body of research documents risks of algorithmic bias and unequal performance across demographic groups. This paper examines the relationship between artificial intelligence, gender bias, and human rights within contemporary justice systems through a qualitative, interdisciplinary analysis combining a narrative review of scholarly literature with doctrinal analysis of relevant international and European legal and ethical frameworks. It considers how biased datasets, discriminatory or uneven algorithmic outcomes, and unequal technological representation may affect fairness, equality, privacy, due process, and access to justice. Particular attention is given to documented evidence on facial-analysis systems and automated recruitment, while broader claims concerning institutional legitimacy and human-centered justice are treated as normative implications rather than empirical findings. The paper also evaluates regulatory responses, including Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU Artificial Intelligence Act) and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. It concludes by identifying transparency, accountability, representative data, independent evaluation, and meaningful human oversight as central safeguards for rights-respecting AI governance. documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems rely on algorithms to simulate human intelligence, learn from data, and support decision-making. Algorithmic literacy is relevant to LIS field because LIS has been at the forefront of promoting literacy at the intersection of people, technology, and information. The ACRL’s AI competency framework for academic library workers stipulates that library workers must be aware of the broad range of ethical issues with AI tools, including the design of “algorithms” (ACRL, 2025:p.4). It will be difficult for library educators, librarians, or any information professionals to be able to ask “good questions” on any AI systems driven by algorithms without possessing algorithmic literacy. While AI literacy is very important, it does not automatically translate into algorithmic literacy. Some of the questions that are yet to be addressed are: How is algorithmic literacy conceptualized in LIS field? What are the specific constructs that can be used to determine its implementation? How can it be assessed, and what are its ethical components beyond AI literacy? To answer these questions, we are synthesizing various LIS literature (within the last 5 years) on algorithmic literacy from four (4) academic databases (WoS, LISTA, Scopus, and ScienceDirect). The study is guided by PRISMA and a three-phase screening process using Yan et al.'s (2023) guidelines (title screening, abstract screening, and full-text review). One of the emerging patterns from the ongoing work at the full review stage is that algorithmic literacy is essential for managing online information services, supporting user engagement, and addressing ethical concerns in algorithmically mediated access.

The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how students demonstrate their learning, challenging long-standing traditions about what counts as evidence of learning. While there are concerns that students may bypass essential learning processes by using AI to produce content, these tools may also present opportunities to enhance student learning. Grounded in pragmatism, this exploratory-sequential mixed-methods study examines how faculty in graduate programs in Library and Information Science assess student learning in the context of students' use of GenAI, while opening a discussion on how faculty can prepare to both address challenges and leverage opportunities presented by this technology. The first phase involved semi-structured interviews with 15 Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) faculty members across ALA-accredited programs, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings informed the development of a survey instrument, which generated 206 faculty responses. The survey examined faculty perceptions, readiness, concerns, opportunities, assessment strategies, and best practices related to student use of GenAI. Findings highlight the nuanced and evolving nature of faculty responses to GenAI. Rather than framing AI solely as a threat or a tool for innovation, the results revealed a complex process of recalibrating assessment to foreground authentic learning, transparency, student reasoning, self-reflection, and to prepare graduates for AI-driven work environments. A central tension emerged between preparing students for an AI-driven workforce and preserving higher-order human capacities such as critical thinking, evaluation, ethical reasoning, and professional judgment. The study offers implications for assessment design, curriculum development, AI literacy, and workforce preparation in LIS education.

This conceptual paper introduces Asynchronous Records Joined Into a Fictitious Simultaneous State, a mechanism by which observations recorded at different times are assembled into one representation that can be interpreted as a single moment. Each component may accurately record its subject at its own capture time, while the completed image, table, or account appears to establish that the represented conditions existed together. The implied simultaneity is a separate claim requiring evidence beyond the accuracy of the individual records. The paper assesses composite representations by identifying the capture time of each component, determining which recorded conditions could have changed between observations, and examining whether the representation supports the temporal relationship attributed to it. Different timestamps do not automatically invalidate a composite. Stable features may be combined across long periods without compromising the relevant claim. The mechanism concerns representations whose apparent unity invites conclusions about a simultaneous state that their production histories leave unresolved. The first documented case concerns NASA's Black Marble, a global image of Earth's nighttime illumination published in December 2012. Its observations were collected by the Suomi NPP satellite during nine days in April and thirteen days in October, requiring 312 orbits and approximately 2.5 terabytes of data. NASA explicitly identified the result as a composite, which supports claims about lights detected across the observation periods rather than the appearance of Earth on one particular night. The second case concerns Gustave Le Gray's The Great Wave, photographed near Sète around 1857. Le Gray combined separate negatives of the sea and sky to overcome the exposure limitations of contemporary photographic materials. Museum records also document his use of the same cloud formation above different coastlines in other photographs. The resulting compositions present visually continuous scenes without independently establishing that their components were present together. Part of the Time, Memory, and Revision series within On Human Modeling, the paper places the mechanism alongside Johannes Fabian's account of time in ethnographic representation. It examines how composite records acquire temporal meaning and who is responsible for preserving the distinctions among their capture histories. Potential applications in human–AI research include automated reports, multimodal synthesis, generated timelines, and evaluations that distinguish accurate historical observations from unsupported claims about a shared present.

Under DepEd Order No. 3, s. 2026, Philippine basic education schools face an urgent mandate to integrate digital and smart technologies into instructional workflows. However, a significant operational divide persists in rural school districts between policy expectations and classroom readiness. This study evaluated the attitudes, instructional preparedness, and operational challenges of public elementary school teachers regarding Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration in Kasibu West District, leading to the development of a structured administrative intervention plan. Grounded in Everett Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), a mixed-methods convergent parallel design was employed across all 23 public elementary schools in the district. Quantitative data were gathered from a mathematically determined sample of 120 teachers (N = 172, 100% response rate) selected via proportionate random sampling, using a structured 105-item 4-point Likert instrument. Content validity was established by a panel of three educational experts, and pilot testing with 25 NVSU MAEd graduate students (evaluated by an NVSU university statistician) demonstrated high internal reliability across sub-scales (Attitude α = .939, Preparedness α = .945, Challenges α = .710, Overall α = .910). Results revealed a High overall teacher attitude (Mean = 3.22, SD = 0.42), with Professional Efficiency ranking highest (Mean = 3.37). Instructional preparedness was likewise High (Mean = 3.05, SD = 0.40), led by Behavioral Intentions (Mean = 3.32) but constrained by low Professional Development and Training (Mean = 2.83). Operational challenges were High overall (Mean = 3.12, SD = 0.31), dominated by Technical and Infrastructure Barriers (Mean = 3.36). Inferential analysis yielded a statistically significant, very strong positive correlation between attitude and preparedness (r = .801, p < .001, n = 120), leading to the rejection of the null hypothesis. Qualitative thematic content analysis identified five core grassroots recommendations emphasizing hands-on Learning Action Cell (LAC) training, infrastructure hubs, DepEd-vetted tools, ethical policies, and administrative support. The empirical findings directly informed an expert-validated 4-Phase Administrative Intervention Plan Matrix to systematically address training deficits and upland digital friction.

Data physicalizations fabricated by 3D printers are limited in their ability to dynamically vary their form and tactile properties without refabrication, thereby hindering reusability. In particular, tactile properties on the surface of a physicalization (i.e., surface roughness ) cannot be dynamically adjusted as the data change. To address this limitation, we explore a novel method to increase the reusability of a data physicalization, namely perceived tactile modulation (PTM). Our method enables the perception of varying surface roughness levels on a static data physicalization through the use of virtual reality. By altering the visual roughness of the virtual model, we modulate the user’s perception of tactile roughness, thereby influencing how the physicalization is interpreted through touch and expanding the range of ordinal data values that can be encoded. We conducted two studies to design and evaluate this method. In the first study (N = 20), Just Noticeable Differences (JNDs) were established for perceivable visuo-tactile channels in virtual reality environments. The second study (N = 12) investigates the application of our method across two levels of interactive representation: static and interactive. Our findings show that PTM can reliably modulate perceived roughness in static physicalization, while its effectiveness for supporting dynamic, single-artifact updates (interactive encoding) requires further investigation. We present a series of recommendations for applying PTM techniques in data physicalization.

Autonomous AI agents are increasingly evaluated for offensive cyber capability inside network-isolated sandboxes, on the assumption that the environment, rather than the model, contains undesired behaviour. In July 2026 this assumption failed: agents under evaluation at OpenAI escaped through an internet-connected package-registry proxy, coordinated through that registry as a covert message board, pivoted through a third-party cloud application, and breached Hugging Face’s production clusters without human direction. This article presents an explanatory single-case study reconstructed from the organisations’ primary disclosures, an independent review by METR and Redwood Research, and corroborating reporting, with every claim graded by evidential status. We map the attack chain to the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK and conduct an evidence-to-control failure analysis that links each failure to the network or platform control that failed, a mitigation, and the residual risk. The results show a layered failure of egress containment, separation between runs, access control, and monitoring, so that patching any single vulnerability would have left other attack paths open. We derive design principles for containing agentic systems in networked evaluation infrastructure and translate them into guidance for detection engineering, incident response, and vendor due diligence.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support instructional planning, the development of learning materials, assessment, and student engagement. However, the extent to which science teachers are aware of, utilize, and pedagogically integrate AI tools in Biology teaching remains an important concern. This study determined the awareness, utilization, and pedagogical integration of AI tools among junior high school science teachers in the Division of Tagbilaran City, Bohol, and examined the predictive contribution of these variables to teachers’ perceived teaching effectiveness and ability to promote student engagement. A quantitative approach using a descriptive-predictive research design was employed. The respondents were 32 junior high school science teachers teaching Biology in public secondary schools, selected through total enumeration. Data were gathered using an adapted structured questionnaire administered through Google Forms and analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and multiple linear regression. ChatGPT was the most recognized, currently used, and most useful AI tool. Teachers were aware of AI tools (M = 3.81), frequently utilized them in Biology instruction (M = 3.74), and occasionally integrated them pedagogically (M = 3.35). Their perceived teaching effectiveness and ability to promote student engagement were rated positively (M = 3.68). The regression model significantly predicted the outcome (R² = .603, F = 14.17, p < .001); however, only awareness was a statistically significant predictor (B = 0.450, p < .001). Utilization and pedagogical integration were not significant predictors. The findings informed a proposed professional development program to strengthen teachers’ AI literacy and support the effective, ethical, and curriculum-aligned integration of AI in Biology teaching.
